summary:
Antioquia department stands under Colombia's national legal framework, which is among the most developed in Latin America. Since a rule change approved in June 2015, trans Colombians change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments; the official who defended the change described those examinations as profoundly invasive of privacy rights and rooted in unacceptable prejudice. Constitutional Court jurisprudence dating from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition on the basis of self-recognition without a surgical requirement, and national identification documents carry trans and non-binary markers from November 2025.

Entry and partner recognition are settled in the visitor's favour. Marriage equality has been available since 2016 and adoption by same-sex couples since 2015. The first same-sex marriage conducted abroad was registered in Colombia in March 2016, and the National Registry issued a memo ordering all notaries and registrars to register same-sex marriages performed outside the country. Same-sex couples married abroad are entitled to the same visa, healthcare benefits, inheritance and pension rights as heterosexual spouses once they present a stamped marriage certificate and identification papers at the nearest designated office.

Access to premises and to state services is covered by court order and administrative decree. Judgments T-314 of 2011 (Tequendama Hotel), T-909 of 2011 (Cosmocentro mall guards in Cali) and T-301 of 2004 (Santa Marta police at the city boardwalk) protect entry to public and commercial premises. A 2011 Constitutional Court ruling allowed a transgender woman prisoner to choose her own hairstyle and makeup, and a Colombian court has since ruled on the treatment of trans detainees. The 2016 Ministry of Interior decree set procedural obligations for government institutions covering LGBTI rights in public education, health care, prisons and as victims of armed conflict, and a May 2018 executive decree by President Juan Manuel Santos extended guarantees to housing, work, recreation, sports and culture.

Against that framework, Antioquia has been the site of a killing that drew national attention. On 5 April 2025 a 28-second video went viral showing 32-year-old trans woman Sara Millerey González Borja beaten and thrown into a waterway in Bello in broad daylight, flailing and unable to swim with fractured legs, arms and hands, while onlookers filmed; she drowned and died of cardiac arrest the following afternoon. Her mother Sandra Borja said they killed her for being who she was. President Gustavo Petro ordered an urgent investigation and solidarity events and protests were held in several cities. A clinic reportedly did not treat her as an emergency because she did not get shot, and Antioquia's regional authorities were criticised for using her pre-transition name. She was the third LGBTQ person killed in Bello in 2025, after two gay men.

Trans-specific killings at scale continue nationally and affect Antioquia. Thirteen trans people were killed in Colombia in the first quarter of 2025 alone. The Attorney General's Office recorded 35 LGBTI murders between January and May 2025. Forty-one transgender women were killed across the country in 2023, with eight more between February and April 2024, figures that also cover Antioquia, and more than 40 trans women were killed in 2023. Reporting describes the violence as calculated brutality persisting amid the country's decades-long civil conflict, with further queer killings recorded after the Millerey case.

Some of the targeting is organised by armed groups. In Guajira, armed groups have posted flyers carrying a kill list of named individuals since March 2024, stating that all will be military targets, including homosexuals, lesbians, rapists and trans people. In Caquetá, where ex-rebel structures persist despite the 2016 peace agreement, flyer campaigns distributed on streets and WhatsApp announce a social cleansing of drug addicts, prostitutes and faggots; trans salon owner Tatiana Cespedes was forced to move twice after death threats from armed men, and trans women in the department have few options beyond sex work.

Protection machinery exists but has not closed the gap. In July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, the state acknowledging conflict-driven violence as gender persecution, a crime against humanity, and the UN Human Rights Committee noted concern. In May 2025 the UN Independent Expert on SOGI violence and discrimination, Graeme Reid, concluded a fact-finding mission across multiple Colombian cities, praising the government's legal reforms while warning of a stark disconnect between institutional progress and daily lived experience, with widespread discrimination and violence requiring urgent attention as killings rise.
tangentialFactors:
Antioquia's risk profile sits within a national pattern in which organised armed structures drive anti-LGBTI intimidation. The flyer campaigns documented in Guajira since March 2024 and in Caquetá during 2024 represent the same tactics of public kill lists and declared social cleansing that trans Colombians in Antioquia may encounter when travelling to those departments; no source in this inventory documents an equivalent flyer campaign inside Antioquia itself.

The political and institutional response has been active but uneven. Presidential intervention, nationwide protests and sustained press coverage followed the Bello killing, while municipal authorities in Antioquia drew criticism for publishing the victim's pre-transition name. That combination of high-level attention and local mishandling is a recurring feature of the cases recorded here.

The violence follows the country's conflict geography rather than a single city. Reporting from Medellín and Bello, from Guajira and from Caquetá describes the same underlying condition: ex-rebel and armed structures operating alongside ordinary urban crime, with trans women bearing a disproportionate share of the resulting fatalities. Comparisons with the national tallies are the only reliable baseline, since Antioquia-specific kill counts are not published in this inventory beyond the Bello cases.

outOfScopeNotes:
No Antioquia-specific source in this inventory covers the national 2023 and 2024 transgender kill tallies or the armed-group flyer campaigns in Guajira and Caquetá; those figures and campaigns are national or other-department findings used here as context for Antioquia, and departmental totals for Antioquia beyond the Bello cases are not sourced.

Whether the clinic's refusal to treat Sara Millerey as an emergency case led to any disciplinary or regulatory outcome is unresolved in the sources provided. Likewise, the current status of the comprehensive trans law reported as under legislative consideration in 2025 is not sourced here.

The inventory does not document whether Antioquia's own departmental or municipal governments maintain trans-specific protection programmes, hate-crime charging practices, or dedicated police units; only the national decrees and national court judgments are sourced. The identification of the individuals filmed at the Bello waterway, and any prosecutions arising from the video, remain unresolved on this record.
